title: SYSK Gets Weird Playlist: Dragons: As Real as Mermaids
summary: Playlist episode 7 of the SYSK Gets Weird series, "Dragons: As Real as Mermaids." The hosts argue that dragons across cultures are not one universal tradition: many ancient 'dragon' references were mistranslated or lazily translated from other creatures. Topics include the theory that David E. Jones's 'An Instinct for Dragons' ties dragons to ancient fears of snakes, cats, and eagles; a theory that the dragon derives from descriptions of bee swarms and honey; Homer's use of 'drakon' for snakes in the Iliad; Sumerian and Akkadian mythic beasts mistranslated as dragons; the Bible's dragon/Satan imagery; Beowulf's dragon; the St. George and crocodile legend (linked to a story also told of St. Theodore); the 1260 AD Western dragon image in MS Harley 3244; Asian (Chinese and Japanese) dragons as benevolent rain and water deities; the artist Chen Rong; and dragons in literature and pop culture such as Tolkien's Smaug, Dungeons & Dragons, Pete's Dragon, and Reign of Fire. The episode closes with a listener mail about corn kernels in a childhood poop incident.
topics: An Instinct for Dragons David E. Jones
fear of predators origin of dragons

segments.title: Episode intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces episode 7 of the SYSK playlist on dragons, 'as real as mermaids,' with a Dragonslayer pun and a sidetrack about Bill Withers and George Benson.

segments.title: Banter and Western vs. Asian dragons
segments.summary: Josh notes that dragon traditions differ across cultures and that claims that every culture has dragons are overstated; the modern idea of dragons was built from varied mythical beasts.

segments.title: Hosts' opening remarks on dragons
segments.summary: Chuck introduces David E. Jones's book An Instinct for Dragons, proposing that dragons combine primate fears of snakes, big cats, and eagles. Josh adds that this fear is evolutionary.
topics: fear of predators origin of dragons

segments.title: Dragons as explanations for natural phenomena
segments.summary: Chuck discusses how ancient cultures used myths to explain weather, volcanoes, and fossil bones such as dinosaur or whale bones, possibly giving rise to dragon stories.

segments.title: Bee swarm dragon theory
segments.summary: Josh describes a theory, without consensus, that ancient descriptions of bee swarms, stings, and honeycomb treasure were metaphors that became dragons.

segments.title: Homer's drakon and the word dragon
segments.summary: Chuck explains that the word dragon traces to Greek drakon, which Homer in the Iliad used for snakes, with later natural history writers also describing the dracon as an enemy of the eagle.

segments.title: Mistranslation and lazy translation
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how writers mixed natural history and myth, and how translators rendered any mythical beast as a dragon, causing mistranslation.

segments.title: Mistranslation wrap-up
segments.summary: Josh argues that lazy translation shaped the idea that every culture has dragons; Chuck praises the point.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with hosts' banter about rose petals and Ned Flanders.

segments.title: Sumerian and Akkadian beasts
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Sumerian legends of the Usum and gods, mistranslated as dragons; scholars who read Akkadian have revealed more nuance.

segments.title: Dragons in the Bible and Paradise Lost
segments.summary: Chuck notes that Revelation describes a great dragon as Satan, with the Greek drakon used; the hosts briefly mention Paradise Lost and the film Red Dragon, drifting into off-topic chat.

segments.title: Greedy treasure-guarding dragons and Beowulf
segments.summary: Chuck describes the typical greedy, vengeful dragon that demands sacrifice; Josh links it to Beowulf's dragon, which guards treasure and was angered by theft of a golden goblet.

segments.title: St. George, St. Theodore and the crocodile
segments.summary: Chuck explains the St. George legend, noting that St. Theodore's story came first through retelling. Josh describes a spring town guarded by a crocodile, fed sheep and then maidens, and says the legend may derive from that real crocodile.

segments.title: MS Harley 3244 and the Western dragon image
segments.summary: Chuck points to the 1260 AD illustration in MS Harley 3244 as an early image of the Western dragon; Josh says it is attributed to William Peralt, likely English, and spread through Europe.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before discussing Asian dragons.

segments.title: Asian dragons as rain and water deities
segments.summary: Josh says Asian dragons are benevolent and tied to rain and water, with parade dragons based on ancient rain ceremonies. Chuck notes Chinese dragon carvings dating back far earlier than Western ones; Josh links them to animism.

segments.title: Dragons in Ghost of Tsushima
segments.summary: Chuck discusses the video game Ghost of Tsushima and its Japanese setting, and Josh mentions the lair of Chinese dragons in ruined temples. Chuck says no dragons have appeared in the game yet.

segments.title: Japanese ryu and Chen Rong
segments.summary: Josh describes the Japanese ryu as a poetry-writing dragon using belly scales as paper, and Chuck recommends the 13th-century painter Chen Rong's dragon art.

segments.title: Chen Rong artwork and Scary Stories
segments.summary: Josh says a Chen Rong work, possibly Nine Dragons at the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, resembles the art in Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark; the hosts joke about copying.
topics: Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark

segments.title: Famous dragons in literature, film and pop culture
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Smaug in Tolkien's The Hobbit, Dungeons & Dragons' colored dragon types, fire-breathing origins, Leviathan, the first dragon in literature in Spenser's The Faerie Queene and Dolnois's The Green Serpent, Pete's Dragon, Reign of Fire, Puff the Magic Dragon, Dragon Ball Z, and Game of Thrones.

segments.title: Closing thoughts
segments.summary: Josh wraps up that all dragon depictions are talking about bees and invites listeners to search for dragons in ruined temples or caves.

segments.title: Listener mail: corn and poop
segments.summary: Mary from Issaquah, Washington, recounts seeing corn kernels in a neighbor toddler's stool when she was about three or four in Houston, and says it ruined corn for her.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh thanks Mary and invites listeners to send in mail to the show's address.
